body.heading: Circling versus written
paragraphs: An unnamed worry expands to fill your whole mind, because it has no edges. Writing it down forces edges onto it: one sentence, in plain words, about one specific thing. “I'm stressed” becomes “I'm worried I'll forget my lines in Friday's assembly.”
The written version may still be a real problem, but it is now a problem with a shape — and shaped problems can be planned for, asked about, or deliberately set aside until Friday.

body.heading: The five-minute worry page
paragraphs: Set a timer for five minutes and write everything on your mind without tidying it up. Then close the notebook. Giving worries a scheduled place and time makes them less likely to interrupt the rest of the day.
This is a self-help habit, not a treatment. If worry is constant, overwhelming, or stopping you sleeping or functioning, a trusted adult or professional can offer far more than a notebook can.

takeaway: Write the worry in one plain sentence, and it becomes a problem with edges.
